title: Delightful Policy Gradient under Distributed Friction
claim: A sequence task is scored per position: the response is compared to the correct output and graded by the fraction of positions it gets right.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right, input beside correct and response rows, braces annotating
description: A single-panel schematic of a toy binary sequence task. On the left, a row of five gray boxes holds the input 1 1 0 1 0, labeled 'Input', with a curly brace above marked 'H = 5' for the sequence length. On the right, two rows of five boxes. The top row, labeled 'Correct', is 0 1 0 1 1 in gray. The bottom row, labeled 'Response', is 0 1 0 0 1. Its first three boxes are green (correct) and its last two are red (wrong). A green brace under the green boxes carries the label 'C = 3 / 5', the fraction correct. The eye goes first to the green and red boxes and the C = 3/5 label. The figure uses large sans-serif text on a white background and has no arrows.
caption: Token reversal (M=2, H=5): the agent must output the input in reverse. Here it gets three correct then errs, giving ck = 3/5 and reward Rk = κ · 3/5.
abstract: Distributed reinforcement learning trains on data from stale, buggy, or mismatched actors, whose actions often have high surprisal (negative log-probability) under the learner's policy. Supervised fine-tuning learns stably from such logged data, while policy gradient often does not. We trace the difference to negative learning from surprising data: rare failures can dominate finite-batch updates, while rare successes carry information the current policy would otherwise miss. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) separates the two by gating each term with delight, the product of advantage and surprisal, and needs no behavior probabilities. In a contaminated bandit, DG suppresses the perpendicular noise of rare failures by a factor that vanishes as the learner improves; no gate based only on learner probability can do this without also suppressing rare successes. On MNIST with stale actors, DG beats importance-weighted policy gradient given the exact behavior probabilities. On a transformer sequence task, DG often reaches an order of magnitude lower error under staleness, actor--learner probability mismatch, actor bugs, reward corruption, and rare discovery. With four frictions combined, its sample-efficiency advantage grows with sequence length. All experiments are controlled diagnostics; we do not evaluate an end-to-end distributed system.
